title: Help families overcome their anxiety about math
description: Another tip from the grantees' experiences is to "help families overcome their anxiety about math." citation: Dalgaard, N. T., Bondebjerg, A., Viinholt, B. C. A., & Filges, T. (2022). The effects of inclusion on academic achievement, socioemotional development and wellbeing of children with special educational needs. Campbell Systematic Reviews, 18, e1291. https://doi.org/10.1002/cl2.1291
title: Hegarty's seven factors associated with positive student outcomes in inclusive settings
description: The review reports, citing Hegarty (1993), a narrative review identifying "a number of factors are associated with positive student outcomes in inclusive settings": instruction based on student achievement needs, materials and procedures allowing students to proceed at their own pace, additional time for students who need it, increased student responsibility for their own learning, co-operation among students in achieving goals, support teaching, and collaboration among special and general education teachers. The pattern describes a configuration of instructional and organisational conditions under which inclusive placements are reported to work well.

constraints: The factors come from a narrative review cited second-hand by this review; the review did not meta-analyse them as moderators
target_learners: children with special educational needs in inclusive general education settings

social adjustment in inclusive classrooms
examples: The review quotes Hegarty's enumerated list of seven factors in its background section on how the intervention might work.

article_title: Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance
citation: Khosravi, H., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., Yan, L., Lodge, J. M., Tangen, J. M., Denny, P., DiCerbo, K., Buckingham Shum, S., & Baker, R. S. (2026). Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04816
title: Four pedagogical principles for AI companion design derived from the HELF
description: Building on the Higher Education Learning Framework, the paper derives four principles for AI companion design: "deep and interactive learning", which prompts learners to actively process and connect new knowledge; "guided scaffolding", delivering adaptive guidance calibrated to the learner's Zone of Proximal Development; "learning to learn and higher-order learning", fostering metacognition, reflection, and autonomy; and "contextual learning", situating learning in authentic contexts for transfer and disciplinary identity. Each principle is elaborated with companion strategies such as prompting generation and retrieval rather than provision, and metacognitive calibration comparing expressed confidence against actual performance.
requirements: Companions must make the student do the thinking rather than remain passive recipients of explanation
constraints: Principles are drawn from the learning sciences literature rather than tested in this paper
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: deep durable understanding
metacognitive skills
transfer
learner autonomy
examples: The paper recommends companions shift fluidly across interactional roles as tutor, peer, or novice to sustain dialogue and perspective-taking

citation: Misan Paul Etchie, Olutosin Taiwo. (2026). AI-Integrated Learning Management System for Middle School: A Longitudinal Study of Learning Outcomes Through High School and Beyond. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07544
title: Give AI assistance under a help-not-answers rule that preserves productive struggle
description: Because answer-giving can short-circuit productive struggle, the article's AI assistance module follows a bounded-support policy: 'It follows a "help, not answers" rule: the goal is to guide students toward the next step with formative feedback and scaffolding, without simply giving away solutions.' Assistance takes the form of targeted hints based on error type, revision-encouraging feedback, reflection prompts, and short conceptual explanations, keeping students doing the thinking rather than supplying solutions.
requirements: Policy constraints such as no direct answers on graded items
Teacher and administrator configurability of AI behavior
Logging of all AI outputs for auditability
constraints: Assistance must be bounded by context (practice vs. assessment), since unrestricted help on graded work would undermine learning and validity of outcomes
target_learners: Middle school students
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding and revision
Productive persistence rather than answer-copying
examples: Practice-mode AI Learning Coach providing guided, stepwise hints with controlled next-hint progression, while AI help is disabled on graded assignments

title: HERO-QA pipeline: hierarchical retrieval, answer generation with abstention, and a structured-output LLM judge
description: HERO-QA is the audit pipeline the article uses to generate and compare answers grounded in different institutional handbooks. The article states it "uses hierarchical BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009) and dense retrieval (Xiao et al., 2024) with reranking, or the full extracted text for short handbooks (≤80,000 characters)." Qwen3-32B generates answers at temperature 0.1 and can return NOT ADDRESSED when evidence is insufficient; a Qwen3-32B judge with structured JSON output assigns a relationship label (ABSENT, CONSISTENT, COMPLEMENTARY, DIVERGENT, CONTRADICTORY), a divergence topic, and a low/medium/high significance rating.
requirements: Retrieval quality and sufficient handbook text; the judge supplies labels, divergence topics, and significance ratings for disagreements
constraints: The article states these ratings describe potential consequences inferred by the model, not observed patient harm, and do not establish clinical correctness; generation and judging use the same model family

target_learning_goals: measuring coverage and disagreement across institutional patient-education corpora before AI deployment

article_title: HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving
citation: Hyoungwook Jin, Weirui Peng, Jieun Han, Q. Vera Liao, and Xu Wang. (2026). HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28918
title: HelpCoach: an in situ chat-interface add-on scaffolding targeted help-seeking
description: HelpCoach is an add-on to chat interfaces that scaffolds students in formulating specific questions during problem solving. It monitors question specificity in real time, assessing whether each question identifies both a knowledge component and a scaffold type, and provides feedback to keep students aware of targeted help-seeking. When a question is not specific, it prompts templated revision with lists of knowledge components and scaffold types, and a scoped-exploration module recommends three relevant knowledge components and three scaffold types from students' code and chat history. Scaffolds fade as students demonstrate targeted help-seeking.
requirements: Requires initial inputs specifying the relevant knowledge components (e.g., via cognitive task analysis, learner-sourcing, or AI generation) and scaffold types for the target task.
constraints: The article expects generalization across domains with well-defined knowledge components, such as mathematics and science, but states it requires initial inputs that specify the relevant knowledge components and scaffold types.
target_learners: college students learning web programming
target_learning_goals: targeted help-seeking during AI-supported problem solving
metacognitive skills of assessing question specificity and selecting scaffolds
examples: In the lab study, HelpCoach participants completed three Vue.js programming tasks with a GPT-5.4-mini chatbot, receiving specificity ratings, templated revision prompts only for non-specific questions, and scoped suggestions marked with a star.

article_title: Students' Perception Accuracy of Partners' AI Use and its Relation to Collaboration Performance
citation: Laura Graf, Ramona Beinstingel, Stephan Krusche, Oleksandra Poquet. (2026). Students' Perception Accuracy of Partners' AI Use and its Relation to Collaboration Performance. Preprint, Technical University of Munich. https://tum.de
title: Heuristic-inference account of partner AI-use beliefs under observability constraints
description: The article proposes that when a coordination-relevant behaviour such as AI use is not directly observable, collaborators form beliefs about partners through heuristic inference rather than partner-specific knowledge. Two heuristics are named: social projection, where "individuals assume partners to be similar to them and use their own behaviour as a reference point for judging others", and normative expectation, assumptions about what behaviour is typical or appropriate in a context. The study's partial-correlation results support the dominance of assumed similarity, reframing AI-use transparency as a coordination resource rather than only an integrity concern.
requirements: Requires a collaboration context where partners' AI use is private and observable work traces no longer distinguish own work from AI generation
constraints: Assumed-similarity effects may be pronounced when partners are already acquainted, as in this sample
The account is supported by observational, self-report data and should not be interpreted causally
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: accurate perception of collaborators' AI use during collaborative programming
effective team coordination in AI-supported collaborative work
examples: In the study, students' estimates of partners' task-level AI use correlated strongly with their own usage profiles (median r = .73), and partner-specific residual accuracy was low

article_title: Beyond Direct Answering: Aligning Educational LLMs as Socratic Guides via Heuristic Reinforcement Learning
citation: Xiaokun Wang, Siyu Song, Wentao Liu, Xiaodong Zou. (2026). Beyond Direct Answering: Aligning Educational LLMs as Socratic Guides via Heuristic Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22996
title: HeuristicEdu: an SFT-then-GRPO alignment pipeline with a three-component heuristic reward for Socratic tutoring
description: HeuristicEdu is a two-phase alignment pipeline that redirects an instruction-tuned LLM from direct answer delivery toward Socratic guided inquiry. Phase 1 is supervised fine-tuning on the SocraticEdu corpus; Phase 2 applies GRPO with the composite reward Rtotal = αRcog + βReng − γRdir, where Rcog measures normalized Bloom's-taxonomy cognitive lift between turns via an LLM judge, Reng scores engagement cues via an Engagement Proxy Model, and Rdir penalizes novel keyword leakage with a Kquery correction for student-introduced terms. The article states "Section 7 shows that γ= 0is optimal in practice", and the pipeline includes inference-time spell correction and intent filtering before evaluation with SE and CD metrics.
requirements: A supervised warm-up corpus of Socratic trajectories (SocraticEdu, 797 trajectories)
An LLM judge for Bloom's levels and an Engagement Proxy Model for reward scoring
Curated keyword sets Ki per seed question for the directness term and leakage evaluation
constraints: The directness penalty Rdir is harmful as a GRPO reward (γ=0 optimal in practice), though explicit term constraints can reduce inference-time leakage
Results are demonstrated on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with a 30-question held-out test set; margins below 0.10 are treated as indicative
target_learners: Chinese primary-school students ages 8-12 in K-12 science platforms
target_learning_goals: Guided discovery of core science concepts through progressive Socratic questioning rather than direct answer delivery
examples: GRPO-aligned model responses open with analogies and exploratory questions (e.g., asking what color the sky is at sunset) rather than direct disclosure of Rayleigh scattering

article_title: Active learning narrows achievement gaps for underrepresented students in undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and math
citation: Theobald Elli J. et al. (2020). Active learning narrows achievement gaps for underrepresented students in undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and math. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1916903117
title: Heads-and-hearts hypothesis: gap reduction requires combining deliberate practice with inclusive teaching
description: The heads-and-hearts hypothesis is the authors' proposed explanation for the extensive variation in active learning's efficacy across studies. It holds that "meaningful reductions in achievement gaps only occur when course designs combine deliberate practice with inclusive teaching". Deliberate practice comprises extensive focused effort on relevant tasks, scaffolded exercises addressing specific deficits, immediate feedback, and repetition; inclusive teaching emphasizes treating students with dignity and respect, communicating confidence in students' ability to meet high standards, and genuine interest in their growth. The authors claim these elements act synergistically for underrepresented students facing stereotype threat, microaggressions, and underpreparation.
requirements: Course designs must combine deliberate practice elements with a classroom culture supporting inclusion
constraints: Explicit and rigorous testing of the heads-and-hearts hypothesis has yet to be done, per the authors
target_learners: Underrepresented minority and low-income undergraduate STEM students
target_learning_goals: Reducing achievement gaps in STEM course performance and retention
examples: The authors note the intensity data are consistent with the deliberate practice element, and cite a chemistry companion course combining belonging interventions with peer-led group problem-solving that narrowed gaps while controlling for self-selection bias

article_title: The effects of over-reliance on AI dialogue systems on students' cognitive abilities: a systematic review
citation: Chunpeng Zhai, Santoso Wibowo and Lily D. Li. (2024). The effects of over-reliance on AI dialogue systems on students' cognitive abilities: a systematic review. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-024-00316-7
title: Cognitive-shortcut (heuristic) account of AI over-reliance
description: The review's explanatory account of why over-reliance arising from ethical issues of AI affects cognitive abilities: users favor efficient cognitive shortcuts, or heuristics, even when AI presents ethical problems. The review states that "individuals increasingly favor fast and optimal solutions over slow ones constrained by practicality", and links this to cognitive biases in which judgments deviate from rationality, producing uncritical acceptance of AI-generated information. It serves as the review's central perspective for organizing how ethical issues translate into dependency and diminished judgment.
requirements: Users must face AI-generated recommendations whose reliability they struggle to assess for the shortcut tendency to operate as described
constraints: The review draws its data from higher education contexts and does not consider cognitive developmental differences across age groups such as teenagers and primary or secondary school students

critical thinking
analytical thinking

article_title: Conversing with pedagogical agents: A phenomenological exploration of interacting with digital entities.
citation: Veletsianos, G. & Miller, C. (2008). Conversing with pedagogical agents: A phenomenological exploration of interacting with digital entities. British Journal of Educational Technology, 39, 6, 969-986. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2007.00797.x
title: Hermeneutic phenomenological inquiry via the four lifeworld existentials for studying human-agent interaction
description: The article applies phenomenological inquiry, which "seeks to examine, understand and interpret observable, yet special events in our everyday life," to human-agent interaction. The experience of any phenomenon is explained through four lifeworld existentials: body, time, space and relations with others. Researchers bracket their preconceptions, treat informant descriptions as true accounts, and derive the essence of the experience through imaginative variation, testing whether each theme is essential. The authors use this lens because interpretive examinations of pedagogical agents have been meager.
requirements: Informants must have experienced the phenomenon in ecologically valid, natural settings rather than artificial experimental conditions
constraints: No one theme is monolithic; the set of derived themes together describe the lived experience
target_learners: learners interacting with conversational agents in electronic learning environments
target_learning_goals: understanding the user experience of conversing with pedagogical agents
examples: The authors analysed two 50-minute phenomenological interviews and 11 written reflections, grouping lived experience descriptions into five theme statements and removing themes one by one to test essentiality.

citation: Bennett JS, Boyle PA, James BD, Bennett DA. (2012). Correlates of health and financial literacy in older adults without dementia. BMC Geriatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2318-12-30
title: Combined health and financial literacy assessment yielding an averaged total literacy score
description: The article describes a literacy assessment composed of nine health literacy questions (e.g., understanding Medicare, medication instructions, interpreting drug risk) and 23 financial literacy questions (numeracy, compound interest, inflation, financial terms such as FDIC, stocks, and mutual funds), all multiple choice or true/false and scored correct/incorrect. Because the tests differed in item count, subscores were "expressed as the percentage correct out of total items (from 0 – 1)" and "The total literacy score was the average of these two percentages." Total literacy had "adequate internal consistency with a Cronbach 's coefficient alpha of 0.77."
requirements: Administered within the Rush Memory and Aging Project annual clinical evaluation beginning in 2008, with items scored correct or incorrect and subscores converted to percentage correct before averaging
constraints: The authors note they did not use common measures such as REALM or TOFHLA, which makes comparison to prior work difficult

target_learning_goals: ability to understand and process health and financial information, concepts, and numeracy

article_title: Measuring the development of inhibitory control: The challenge of heterotypic continuity
citation: Petersen, I. T., Hoyniak, C. P., McQuillan, M. E., Bates, J. E., & Staples, A. D. (2016). Measuring the development of inhibitory control: The challenge of heterotypic continuity. Developmental Review, 40, 25-71. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dr.2016.02.001
title: Heterotypic continuity of inhibitory control: the same underlying construct changes its behavioral manifestation across development, with two implications for measurement
description: The review's organizing framework is heterotypic continuity, defined as "the manifestation of the same underlying process through different behavioral presentations at different developmental periods". Inhibitory control is continuous in function but appears differently in toddlers (e.g., using words rather than physical aggression to get a toy) than in older children (e.g., inhibiting an action despite social pressure). Self-regulation also shifts from reliance on external sources of control to internal, self-initiated control. The framework yields two measurement implications: the same measure may not reflect the same construct at different ages, and describing heterotypic continuity may require using different measures across time.
requirements: Longitudinal measurement must be guided by theory and construct validity, with attention to developmental appropriateness, developmental sensitivity, and construct validity across the study's time frame
constraints: Scores on the same measure across time may reflect changes in the measure's meaning rather than real construct change; the framework applies to domains showing heterotypic continuity
target_learners: children from toddlerhood through adolescence
target_learning_goals: valid longitudinal assessment of inhibitory control and self-regulation development

article_title: The Relationship Between Tutoring Mode and Learners’ use of Help Tools in Distance Education
citation: Bruno De Lièvre, Christian Depover & Pierre Dillenbourg. (2006). The relationship between tutoring mode and learners' use of help tools in distance education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-6076-4
title: Treat help tools as a set of distinct functions rather than a single concept with a single effect
description: The article's results diverge across the four help tool categories: proactivity raised metacognitive and lexical help use, left conceptual help unchanged, and HT presence reduced navigational help use. The authors conclude that "Help should therefore not be considered as a single concept having a single eﬀect, but rather as a set of distinct functions." Designers should therefore evaluate and support each help function separately.

constraints: Effects of a given tutoring mode differ by help type; a mode that stimulates one function may not stimulate another
target_learners: distance education learners in higher education
target_learning_goals: effective use of integrated help resources during independent learning
examples: In the experiment, proactive tutoring stimulated metacognitive and lexical help use but not conceptual or navigational help use

article_title: Teacher Expectations and Self-Determination Theory: Considering Convergence and Divergence of Theories
citation: Lisette Hornstra, Kim Stroet, Christine Rubie-Davies, Annaline Flint. (2023). Teacher Expectations and Self-Determination Theory: Considering Convergence and Divergence of Theories. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09788-4
title: High expectation theory's three key principles: mixed/flexible grouping, class climate, and goal setting
description: High expectation theory describes three interconnected principles teachers use to communicate high expectations to all students: "mixed ability or flexible grouping (coupled with high-level learning opportunities), class climate, and goal setting." Mixed grouping reduces the salience of ability and provides high-level learning opportunities for all, including high-level questions asked of every student. Class climate involves warm teacher-student relationships, peer support, and collaboration rather than reward for out-performing others. Goal setting gives all students clear learning goals, success criteria, and frequent targeted feedback tied to progress toward those goals.
requirements: Teachers hold beliefs that all students can achieve at high levels given a supportive classroom environment, so expectations are high for all students relative to achievement
constraints: HET does not encompass classroom clarity in the sense of clear rules and expectations as proposed in SDT's notion of structure

article_title: Measurement of some abilities in scientific thinking.
citation: Herring, J. P. (1918). Measurements of some abilities in scientific thinking. The Journal of Educational Psychology, IX(10), 535-558.
title: Herring's analysis of scientific method into eleven measurable abilities
description: The article defines scientific method as "a complex of processes used in the attempts to explain," analyzable but neither finally nor universally, since scientists alter its use across ages and fields. high school pupils

title: Evaluate education policies on intervention benefits and costs, not on the heritability of educational attainment
description: Interpretive principle for education policy: heritability estimates describe a population variance decomposition, and "the heritability of educational attainment per se is not relevant for evaluating the likely consequences of some change to education systems or policy". title: Herrington and Oliver's nine critical characteristics of authentic learning environments
description: The article adopts the framework of Herrington and Oliver (2000), which identifies nine critical characteristics of an authentic learning environment: authentic context, authentic activities, access to expert performances, multiple roles and perspectives, collaborative construction of knowledge, reflection, articulation, coaching and scaffolding, and authentic assessment within tasks. constraints: Implementing all nine elements in a single course can be especially complex for the teacher and involve higher student dedication than the course credit-load

collaboration and communication
intrinsic motivation and engagement

description: Healthy Conversation Skills (HCS) is an approach to behaviour change that trains healthcare professionals to communicate in a person-centred way, exploring patients' context and supporting them to find their own solutions. title: Make patient counseling and preventive information dissemination explicit job responsibilities of primary care physicians

title: Helping Babies Breathe (HBB) simulation-based neonatal resuscitation training program
description: Helping Babies Breathe is "a simulation-based neonatal resuscitation program for low resource settings" focused on the initial resuscitation steps and bag-and-mask ventilation within the first 60 seconds after birth (The Golden Minute). Its materials include a Learner Workbook, a Facilitator Flip Chart, an Action Plan poster with color-coded care paths, and the NeoNatalie neonatal simulator, whose evaluation signs (cry, breathing, heart rate, chest rise) trainers can manipulate. Skills are assessed with a 17-item Knowledge Check, a BMV performance test, and OSCE A and OSCE B scenarios derived from the NRP megacode. In this study it was delivered through a two-level master-trainer cascade with a maximum 6:1 trainee-trainer ratio, three-day hands-on facility courses, and refresher training.
requirements: Trained facility-level master trainers (at least one per facility) and sufficient ventilation equipment for delivery rooms and resuscitation practice corners
Standard HBB assessment tools (Knowledge Check, BMV skills test, OSCE A and OSCE B) for pre- and post-testing
constraints: The article notes published evidence for simulation-based resuscitation training is of very low quality and no published evidence exists for improvement in patient outcome
target_learners: Facility birth attendants (physicians and nurses) in low- and middle-income countries
Facility-level master trainers in pediatrics, obstetrics, anesthesia, and nursing
target_learning_goals: Neonatal resuscitation knowledge and decision-making
Bag-and-mask ventilation skills within the first minute after birth
examples: Three-day on-site facility courses with no didactic sessions, maximal hands-on skill training, paired practice, and a maximum ratio of six BAs per MT

title: Hendry and Ginns' Self-Directed Learning Readiness Scale (SDLRS) with four subscales
description: Hendry's and Ginns' Self-Directed Learning Readiness Scale is a 36-item instrument rated on a 5-point Likert scale from 'Strongly Disagree' to 'Strongly Agree', validated on medical students. article_title: Voluntary peer-led exam preparation course for international first year students: Tutees' perceptions.
citation: Huhn D, Eckart W, Karimian-Jazi K, Amr A, Herzog W, Nikendei C. (2015). Voluntary peer-led exam preparation course for international first year students: Tutees' perceptions. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-015-0391-5
title: HeiTiMed voluntary peer-led exam preparation course for international first-year medical students
description: A voluntary, weekly, peer-led exam preparation course at the University of Heidelberg for first-year international medical students, developed using Kern's curriculum development principles after focus groups with 10 students. "In the first semester, 17 sessions took place in total, i.e. on a weekly basis for the 15 semester weeks with two additional dates included to meet the students' demands." Sessions of at least 2.5 h used tutor-designed PowerPoint presentations, fill-in-the-blank texts, short tests and mock exams, plus space for questions about university and private challenges. Of an estimated 36 international students, 22 attended (61%).
requirements: Two independently leading peer tutors with training in technical and didactic content
Learning objectives defined per session covering cognitive proficiency, medical terminology, confidence and social support
constraints: Participation was voluntary and enrolment free; the evaluation covered one cohort at one faculty
target_learners: First-year international medical students
target_learning_goals: Essential knowledge and skills for first-semester tests and exams
Familiarity with living and studying in a German city
examples: 22 of an estimated 36 international first-year students attended, and 20 completed 319 evaluation questionnaires across the 17 sessions
